t.7.17.1: Then, O king, the mighty-armed Rāvaṇa, roaming over the surface of the earth, reached the forest of Himavat and wandered about there.
t.7.17.2: There he saw a maiden wearing the black antelope skin and matted locks, devoted to the rites prescribed by the seers, practising austerities like a goddess.
t.7.17.3: Seeing that maiden, endowed with beauty and devoted to a very great vow, he, his mind overcome by desire and infatuation, questioned her as if laughing.
t.7.17.5: Whose daughter are you, O gentle lady, and who is your husband, O sinless one? Tell me quickly, as I ask: what is the reason for your pursuit of austerity?
t.7.17.4: Why, gentle lady, do you follow this way of life, so contrary to your youth? This conduct is surely not fitting for this beauty of yours.
t.7.17.6: Thus addressed by that ignoble Rākṣasa, the maiden, rich in austerities, first duly offered him hospitality and then spoke.
t.7.17.7: My father was the righteous brahmarṣi named Kuśadhvaja, the illustrious son of Bṛhaspati, equal to Bṛhaspati in wisdom.
t.7.17.8: From that great-souled one, as he was constantly engaged in the recitation of the Vedas, I was born, a maiden made of speech, known by the name Vedavatī.
t.7.17.9: Then the Devas, together with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas and Pannagas, they too went to my father and sought my hand in marriage.
t.7.17.10: And my father did not give me to them, O lord of the Rākṣasas. I shall tell you the reason for that; listen, O mighty-armed one.
t.7.17.11: My father's desired son-in-law was indeed Viṣṇu, the best of the gods, the lord of the three worlds; therefore my father would not give me to any other.
t.7.17.13: Then my mother, grief-stricken and most noble, embraced that body of my father and entered the fire together with him.
t.7.17.12: The righteous one wished to give me away. Hearing that, the king of the Daityas named Śambhu, proud of his strength, then became enraged, and by that wicked one my father was slain at night as he lay asleep.
t.7.17.14: Therefore this resolve of mine is firmly fixed in my heart: 'I shall make true my father's cherished wish concerning Nārāyaṇa.'
t.7.17.15: "Even though my father has gone to the realm of the departed, I will accomplish what he longed for": having taken this vow, I practise vast austerity.
t.7.17.16: All this has been told to you by me, O bull among Rākṣasas. Know that I have taken refuge in dharma out of my desire to have Nārāyaṇa as my husband.
t.7.17.17: You are known to me, O king; go, O delight of the Paulastyas. Through my austerity I know everything that exists in the three worlds.
t.7.17.18: Then Rāvaṇa, tormented by the arrows of Kandarpa, descended from the top of his aerial chariot and spoke there to that maiden of exceedingly great vows.
t.7.17.19: You are proud indeed, O lady of lovely hips, you whose mind is set on such a course. O fawn-eyed one, it is in the aged that the gathering of dharma shines.
t.7.17.20: You are endowed with every virtue, the beauty of the three worlds, O timid one; you ought not to take up in your youth such a way of life as is fit only for old age.
t.7.17.21: And who, then, is this one whom you call Viṣṇu? In valour, in austerity, in enjoyment and in strength, he whom you desire is not equal to me, O good lady, O fair one.
t.7.17.22: "No, no, not so!" the maiden said to that night-wanderer; but the rākṣasa seized her by the hair with the tips of his fingers.
t.7.17.23: Then Vedavatī, enraged, cut off her hair with her hand; having kindled a fire, she, hastening toward death, spoke.
t.7.17.25: Since I, though sinless, have been violated by you as if I were a woman without a protector, I shall be born again for the sake of your destruction.
t.7.17.24: Since I have been defiled by you, O ignoble one, my life is now at an end. Therefore, O demon, I shall enter the fire while you look on.
t.7.17.26: Indeed, O sinful one, you cannot be slain by a woman, you above all; and if I were to release a curse upon you, my ascetic power would be wasted.
t.7.17.28: Having spoken thus, she entered the blazing fire, and from the sky a divine shower of flowers fell all around.
t.7.17.27: If there is anything I have done, given, or offered in sacrifice, then by its merit may I be born, not from any womb, as the virtuous daughter of a righteous man.
t.7.17.30: Thus this most fortunate one is born again among mortals, like a flame of fire upon the altar, in a field furrowed by the tip of the plough.
t.7.17.29: She it was through whom that enemy, already struck down long before by her wrath, was slain by you, relying on your superhuman valor, mighty as a mountain.
t.7.17.31: She who was formerly, in the Kṛta age, named Vedavatī has, upon the coming of the Tretā age, arisen again for the slaying of that rākṣasa; because she sprang forth from a furrow, she is now called Sītā by men.
